en: The First Chapter.
Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa! [He who is] the knower of the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, the best among those who know all the Vedas.
The Prajāpati named Dakṣa was a master of all branches of knowledge.
For the benefit of these— the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic— Dakṣa composed this treatise.

A child, from the moment of birth until the age of eight years, should be known as equal to a fetus, being merely a manifestation of its potential. Regarding what is fit or unfit to eat, what is fit or unfit to drink, what should or should not be spoken, and likewise regarding falsehoods— [the child is exempt].
At that time, no fault exists as long as he has not been initiated (upanīta).
Once initiated, there is fault for performing censurable acts;
however, he remains one who has not attained legal capacity until he is sixteen years of age.

When he accepts the Veda and observes the Vedic vows, he is a *brahmacārī*; thereafter, having performed the ritual bath (*snāta*), he becomes a householder. Indeed, two kinds of *brahmacārīs* are recorded in the scripture by the wise.
The first is the *upakurvāṇaka*, while the second is known as the *naiṣṭhika*.
He who, having entered the stage of the householder, becomes a celibate student once again—neither an ascetic nor a forest-dweller—is one who has abandoned all stages of life. (1.7–1.8)
A twice-born man should not remain even for a single moment without belonging to an āśrama;
for he who remains without an āśrama becomes liable to penance.
Indeed, he who is devoted to recitation, burnt offerings, charity, and the study of his own Veda [is exempt].
Even while performing [his duties], he does not obtain that fruit if he has fallen away from his stage of life (āśrama).
For there is regularity among the three [higher castes], but no inverse order;
there is no one more wicked than he who proceeds by way of the inverse order.
One is recognized as a *brahmacārin* by means of the girdle, deerskin, and staff;
a *gṛhastha* by the sacrifices to the gods and so forth; a forest-dweller (*vanāśramin*) by [the growth of] nails and hair;
and an ascetic (*yati*) by the triple staff—each having their own distinct characteristics.
He who lacks these characteristics is neither one who has performed penance nor one belonging to an āśrama. Time was not prescribed by the sages according to the sequence of ritual acts;
however, for the benefit of the twice-born, Dakṣa himself declared it.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Dharmaśāstra of Dakṣa.
The second chapter:
What must be performed daily by a twice-born man after rising in the morning.
I shall explain all of that which is beneficial for the twice-born:
how a Brahmin may not become momentary [in his spiritual state] from sunrise until sunset,
provided he is free from obligatory and occasional rites, as well as from optional rites and those that are censured.
That twice-born man who, out of ignorance or greed, abandons his own duty and performs something else, becomes fallen because of that. Now,
the duty for him during the first part of the day is prescribed.
In the second, third, fourth, and likewise in the fifth,
sixth, seventh, and eighth divisions respectively—
I shall declare in their entirety whatever rites pertain to these various divisions.
When the time of dawn has arrived, one should perform purification according to the rules;
thereafter, one should perform a bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
This body is exceedingly impure and endowed with nine openings.
It flows indeed day and night; one becomes pure by means of the morning bath.
For while one is fast asleep, the senses become moistened and flow, and the limbs reach a state of equality with the lowest parts. (2.7–2.8)
A man who has risen from bed, covered with saliva and sweat,

should not perform any rite— such as recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), or the like— without having first bathed. (2.9) That Brahmin who, having risen in the morning, always performs his morning ablution...
One dispels the sin accumulated over an entire lifetime in three years. That bath which is performed at dawn, at the twilight, and when the sun has risen,
is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and destroys all sins.
They praise the morning bath, for it produces both visible and invisible results.

One who has purified his soul by bathing in the morning is worthy of performing all [rites], such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*). Immediately after the bath, the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*) is prescribed.
By this very procedure, one who has sipped water attains purity. Having washed his feet and hands, he should drink water that has been inspected three times;
then, having wiped [his mouth] with the base of the thumb, he should wipe his face twice.
Having first brought the three [fingers] together, he should thus touch his mouth;
then, having sprinkled his feet, he should touch his limbs.
Immediately thereafter, he should touch his nose with the thumb and the forefinger.
With the thumb and the ring finger, he should repeatedly touch the eyes and the ears;
with the little finger and the thumb, the navel; with the palm, the heart; and finally, with all the fingers, he should touch the head, and with the tips of the fingers, the arms.
If a Brahmin, especially one who is a student (*sādhya*), does not perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) both at dawn and at midday,
he is indeed a Śūdra while still alive and, upon death, is born as a dog. (2.18)
One who omits the twilight devotions is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other rite he performs, he shall not partake of its fruit.
At the conclusion of the twilight rites, however, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) by oneself is prescribed.
Whatever fruit may arise from performing the oblation oneself, that is not produced by another.
A priest, a son, a teacher, a brother, a sister’s son, or a wife’s brother—whatever is offered by these is indeed as if offered by oneself. (2.20–21)
Then, having performed the rites for the gods, one should perform the auspicious inspection.
These duties should be performed with diligence: those for the gods in the forenoon, those for humans at midday, and those for the ancestors in the afternoon. (2.22)
If one should perform that rite which belongs to the forenoon in the evening,
one does not obtain its fruit, just like sexual intercourse with a barren woman.
However, one should perform all of this during the first part of the day.
And in the second part of the day, the study of the Vedas is prescribed.
For the study of the Vedas is said to be the supreme austerity for Brahmins;
that which is accompanied by the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) is to be known as the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña). || 2.24–2.25 ||
First, the acquisition of the Vedas, then reflection, practice, recitation,
and finally teaching them to disciples— thus the study of the Vedas is fivefold.
That time is declared to be for gathering sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and other such items.
And likewise, in the third part of the day, one should accomplish the welfare of those who are to be supported.
Mother, father, teacher, wife, offspring, the poor, those who have sought refuge, as well as the newcomer and the guest—these are declared to be the group of those to be supported. (2.27–28)
Relatives, kinsmen, the destitute, those who have no protector and have sought refuge,
and others who are lacking wealth— this group is declared to be the "class of dependents. The maintenance of this class of dependents is praised as a means for attaining heaven.

There is torment in hell for him; therefore, one should support him with effort. Food and other provisions must especially be prepared for all beings, and they should be given to those who possess knowledge; otherwise, one shall go to hell.

He alone truly lives who, being one, is supported by many; others, however, who merely fill their own bellies, are dead even while they live. Some live for the sake of many, and others likewise for the sake of their families.

One who is distressed even by his own belly is not able to act for the sake of others. (2.33) One who desires prosperity must give to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished. Those who have not given gifts are born to live off the fortune of others. (2.34)
Whatever one gives to distinguished persons and whatever one offers as oblations day by day—that indeed I consider to be wealth; the remainder one merely guards for someone else.
And likewise, in the fourth part [of the day], one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing.
One should bathe in natural water using sesame seeds, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth.
Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). Among these, that which is the daily bathing is further divided into three types.
The removal of impurities is prescribed next with mantras while in the water;
the twilight bath (*sandhyā-snāna*) consists of both of these, and thus the various types of baths are proclaimed.
Within the water, there is the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), and from that, the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Following that, the attendance [upon the teacher] and the recitation of the Sāvitrī are prescribed.
(2.39) That [verse] whose deity is Savitṛ, whose mouth is Agni, and which has three feet; whose seer is Viśvāmitra and whose meter is Gāyatrī—that is distinguished as the Sāvitrī. (2.40)
And likewise, in the fifth portion, a distribution is prescribed according to what is fitting for the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and those who proclaim his fame.
By means of these, he is sustained by the gods, humans, and even animals.
Because the householder performs [these duties] every day, therefore the householder is the senior among the stages of life (āśrama).
Indeed, the householder is said to be the source of the other three stages;
when he falters, those other three also falter. (2.42–43)
The root-prāṇa becomes the trunk; from the trunk come the branches and the sprouts.
When that single root is destroyed, everything perishes.
Therefore, with every effort, the householder must be protected.

He is always to be honored and respected by the king and the other three [orders]. (2.45) Even though he is a householder, one engaged in ritual action does not become a true "house-dweller" merely by virtue of his home, nor by his sons and wife, if he has abandoned his own duty. (2.46)

A man who neither bathes, nor offers oblations, nor recites prayers, nor gives gifts, becomes a debtor to the gods and others and falls into hell. (2.47) For one person alone eats food, while another is eaten by that very food.
He alone does not eat who eats food in the presence of witnesses;
he who is constantly inclined toward sharing, endowed with patience, devoted to compassion, and intent upon the gods and guests—he is a righteous householder. (2.48–2.49)
Compassion, modesty, forgiveness, faith, wisdom, yoga, and gratitude—
he who possesses these qualities is called the foremost householder. (2.50) Having first made a distribution [of his wealth], the householder should be one who eats only what remains.
Having eaten, one should remain at ease and digest that food.
One should spend the sixth and seventh parts of the day with the study of Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth.
During the eighth part, however, one should attend to worldly affairs; thereafter follows the external twilight ritual (saṃdhyā). || 2.51–2.52 ||
Having performed his meal and whatever other domestic duties there may be,
he should thereafter engage in some private Vedic study (svādhyāya).
He should spend the first and last watches of the night in the practice of the Vedas.

For one who sleeps for two watches [of the night] is fit for becoming Brahman. Whenever occasional or optional rites present themselves, they must be performed exactly as they arise; no specific time is prescribed for them.
For one who applies himself to this very [practice] is dissolved into this very [reality].
Therefore, by every effort, it should be performed by one who desires happiness.
(2.56) Throughout [the day], the two middle watches [are for study]; and whatever remains of the oblation after the fire-sacrifice—
"Whether eating or lying down, the Brāhmaṇa does not perish.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Dākṣa Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Three.

For a householder, there are nine kinds of nectar, nine virtuous expenditures, and likewise nine duties; similarly, there are nine forbidden acts. There are nine other things that should be kept secret, and likewise nine that should be made public.
Nine things are fruitful, and nine indeed are fruitless. (3.2) Nine other kinds of objects are always not to be given away;
these nine groups of nine have been specified as bringing prosperity to the householder. (3.3)
I shall describe the "substances of nectar" (sudhāvastūni) to be offered when a distinguished guest has arrived at one's home:
one should offer the fourfold gift of a pleasant mind, eye, face, and speech.
Rising from one's seat, saying "Please come here," and initiating a conversation filled with kindness—these are the acts of hospitality.
These duties—attending upon him and following after him—should be performed with diligence.
(3.5) Furthermore, there are other minor gifts: land, water, grass, washing of the feet, as well as oil for anointing, a seat, and a bed. (3.6)
He should not stay in his house without eating, even if he must provide some food according to his ability;
water for cleansing should also be given to one who asks, and these things should always be present in the home.
(3.7) Sandhyā prayers, ritual bathing, recitation, fire offerings, Vedic study, and worship of the deities—
Likewise, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering and hospitality for guests, or provide water according to his ability (3.8).
He should distribute food as is appropriate among the gods, ancestors, humans, those who are masterless, ascetics, and his mother, father, and teachers (3.9).

These nine are forbidden acts (*vikarma*); furthermore, there is falsehood, adultery, and the eating of forbidden food; as well as approaching women who should not be approached, drinking what should not be drunk, theft, and violence.
Performing rituals not sanctioned by the Vedas and acting contrary to the duties of friendship—these nine are forbidden acts;
one should always avoid them.
[One should likewise conceal] one's lifespan, wealth, domestic secrets, sacred mantras, sexual intercourse, and medical treatments.
Asceticism, giving, and honor—these nine must be guarded with effort:
the application [of means], the clearing of debt, giving, study, and sale;
the giving away of a daughter, the release of a bull, and secret, contemptible sin. (3.13)
These nine things should always be made manifest by those in the householder stage of life:
[giving] to one's mother and father, to a teacher, to a humble friend, and to a benefactor;
and what is given to the helpless, the destitute, and the distinguished becomes fruitful.
What is given to a rogue, a panegyrist, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, or to flatterers,
actors, and thieves, becomes fruitless. (3.16) Common property, what is requested, a deposit, a pledge, a wife, a friend, and wealth— [these are not to be given].
An inheritance received in succession, a deposit, and one's entire property when there is a lineage—
these nine things must never be given away even in times of distress.
The man who gives them away is a fool and shall be subject to penance.
Prosperity never forsakes that man who knows ever-new truths and is devoted to spiritual practice, both in this world and in the next.
One who desires happiness should regard others exactly as one regards oneself.
Pleasures and pains are equal; as they are toward oneself, so they are toward others.
Whatever pleasure or pain is inflicted upon another, all of that will later return to oneself. (3.20–3.21)
Without affliction there is no substance; how can there be action in one devoid of substance?
How can there be dharma in one devoid of action; how can there be happiness in one devoid of dharma?
Everyone desires happiness, and that arises from dharma. (3.22)
Therefore, dharma must always be practiced with effort by all social classes.
With wealth acquired through righteous means, one should perform rites for the sake of the next world;
and gifts should be given according to the rules, at the proper time, and to a worthy recipient endowed with good qualities.

The distinction in the fruit of giving is respectively equal, double, and thousandfold, and infinite; for in the case of injury, the result is exactly the same. (3.25) A gift to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; a gift to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin yields double.

The merit is a thousandfold when given to a teacher, but infinite when given to one who has mastered the Vedas. Likewise, if one gives a gift to an unworthy recipient who lacks the prescribed conduct, not only does that gift perish, but his other merits also perish.
One should give when asked for the sake of remedying a calamity or for the purpose of maintaining a family;
having investigated thus, one should give—for this is the rule for all gifts.
But one who is deprived of mother and father [should be supported] by means of sacraments, marriage, and so forth.
The measure of merit for one who establishes [such a shrine] here is not known.
That welfare which is attained by a man through the establishment of a Brahmin is not obtained by means of the Agnihotra sacrifice, nor by the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (3.29–30)
"Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is beloved in the home—
that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtue by him who desires that [gift] to be imperishable. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Dākṣa-dharmaśāstra*.
The Fourth Chapter:
The home of men has its foundation in the wife, provided she is compliant with their wishes;
there is nothing superior to the householder’s stage of life if the wife is submissive to her husband's will.

Through her, one enjoys the fruit of the threefold aims known as dharma, artha, and kāma. But if she persists in her desire while being restrained out of affection, she will inevitably become uncontrollable later on, like a neglected disease.
For she is compliant, free from verbal fault, skillful, virtuous, sweet-spoken, self-restrained, and devoted to her husband; she is a goddess, not a mere mortal.
For him who possesses a wife so well-disposed, heaven exists even here on earth.
For one whose wife is hostile, there is no doubt that hell awaits;
even in heaven, such mutual affection is indeed difficult to find. What could be more painful than for one to be full of passion while the other is dispassionate?
Household life is for the sake of happiness, and that happiness has its root in the wife;
she is a true wife who is modest, understands the mind [of her husband], and remains obedient. For other women are always miserable and distressed, with mutual discord between their hearts.
Especially for one with two wives, the wife who is hostile [is a source of suffering].
Like leeches, all women—despite being constantly provided with ornaments, clothing, and food, and even with great prosperity—indeed drag a man down. 4.7–4.8
The leech, being solely desirous of blood, takes only the blood;
but the woman takes wealth, the mind, the flesh, the virility, and likewise pleasure.
She is full of apprehension in childhood, and in youth she is intent upon the objects of the senses.
In old age, a woman regards her own body as mere straw.
(4.10) One who is ever-favorable, joyful, skillful, virtuous, and devoted to her husband—a woman endowed with such qualities is indeed Fortune herself; of this there is no doubt. (4.11)
She whose mind is always joyful, who is discerning regarding her station and conduct, and who brings delight to her husband—she is a wife; any other is merely old age.
A student, a wife, a child, a brother, a friend, a servant, and one who has sought refuge [are all to be protected].
For he with whom these are well-disciplined indeed possesses honor in the world. (4.13) The first wife should be the partner in dharma; the second increases pleasure.
In that case, the fruit is seen [in this life] alone; no unseen [fruit] arises. (4.14)

She is declared to be a lawful wife if she remains faultless; if a fault exists, there shall be no offense [in replacing her], and another woman endowed with virtues should be taken. He who abandons a faultless and submissive wife during her youth—
At the end of her life, she shall experience widowhood as if it were a wife's [fate].
(4.16) She who disregards her husband—whether he be poor, diseased, or foolish—shall in this very world become, once again, a female dog, a vulture, and a sow. (4.17)
The woman who, upon her husband's death, ascends the funeral pyre,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so does she rescue her husband from the ocean of worldly existence.
In that same way, having raised up her husband, she rejoices together with him.
(4.19) Outcasts, those who have returned from outcast status, wandering mendicants, and ascetics—the offspring born of these should be made to dwell together with outcasts. (4.20)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Dharmaśāstra of Dakṣa.
Chapter Five:
Purity and impurity have been described; these must be practiced or abandoned by the wise.
Out of a desire for their welfare, I shall state something further regarding the distinction between these two.
(5.1) Effort must always be made toward purity; a twice-born man is remembered as being rooted in purity.
For one devoid of purity and proper conduct, all ritual acts are fruitless. (5.2)
Purity is said to be of two kinds: external and likewise internal.
External purity is traditionally held to consist of earth and water, while the other is the purification of one's inner disposition.
Indeed, external purity is better than impurity; therefore, internal purity is superior.

He who is pure by both [means] is truly pure; no other is pure. (5.4) One application of clay on the penis, three on the anus, ten on the left hand, five on the lower part of the body, ten on one [hand], and seven on both hands. (5.5)

The purification for householders has been declared; for the other three [orders], it is respectively double, triple, and fourfold for the fourth. The first application of clay is prescribed to be the measure of half a handful.
The second and third [fingers] are proclaimed to be half that size.
It is declared here that the cleansing of the penis is accomplished by that which fills three finger-joints.
This is the purification for householders; it is double for students (*brahmacārin*).

Three times as much water should be given to those living in the forest, and four times as much to ascetics, so that the state of the earth becomes neutralized by the clay. Through clay and water, purification shall be achieved without hardship or expenditure of wealth.
The conduct of one who is lax even regarding purification has been examined.
(5.10) One rule for purification is prescribed for the day, another for the night;
one is specified for times of distress, and indeed another for times when there is no distress. (5.11)
The purification prescribed for the day is said to be half that at night;
half of that is prescribed for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey. One who desires purity should not perform less or more than the prescribed purification.
"One should be joined with penance when a prescribed rule has been transgressed.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Dākṣa Dharmaśāstra.
The sixth chapter begins.
I shall now declare *sūtaka* (impurity) caused by birth and death,
as well as the third [type] pertaining to life itself, in due order and according to the rules:
immediate purification, as well as one day, two, three, and four days.
Ten days, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month;
as well as another for the purpose of death—these are the ten types of *sūtaka* (impurity).
I shall describe them all in their proper order without omission.

He who understands the meaning of the texts— the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), along with the ritual manuals (kalpas) and secret doctrines (rahasyas)— and who is devoted to the performance of rites, is not rendered impure by birth or death.
The same applies to kings, officiating priests, and those consecrated for sacrifice, as well as for children and those residing in another country.

Immediate purification is ordained for those observing vows and for those engaged in sacrificial sessions (sattra). A Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires and is learned in the Vedas becomes pure after one day;
likewise, for one who is deficient in these and more deficient still, it is two, three, and four days respectively.

A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a king (Kṣatriya) in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. He who eats without having bathed, without having offered oblations, and without having given gifts, [is likewise impure].
For all such persons as these, there is impurity (sūtaka) for as long as they live:
for one who is diseased, for one who is miserly, for one who is burdened by debt at all times,
for one who is devoid of religious rites, and especially for one who is dominated by women.
For one whose mind is attached to vices, who is perpetually dependent on others,
and who is devoid of faith and renunciation, birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall last until the end of his ashes.
Birth-impurity shall never occur for [the other], whereas for this one, it lasts as long as life itself.
Impurity is declared to be of such specific qualities.
In the case of birth-impurity, death-impurity, and likewise death-impurity following birth-impurity—
for those whose purity is thus combined, purification occurs through the death-impurity alone.
Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended;
however, after ten days, a Brahmin who knows the Dharma deserves ritual purity.
Furthermore, gifts should be given according to the rules, for they deliver one from impurity.
He who dies at the end of a period of impurity caused by death, or she who gives birth at the end of a period of impurity caused by birth—
such a person is purified by the preceding period of impurity for those whose purity is thus consolidated;
however, in both cases, the food of the family must not be eaten for ten days.
On the fourth day, the collection of the bones should be performed by the twice-born.
After the collection of the bones, purification of the limbs is prescribed.
When there is but one husband for women of the various classes in the direct order of castes...
Upon a birth, the period of impurity (sūtaka) shall last ten days, six days, three days, or one day. Likewise,
during the time of a sacrifice, at a wedding, and similarly when there is a divine conjunction,
as well as while the fire is being offered oblations, there is neither ritual impurity nor birth-impurity.

"But all this impurity is proclaimed for times of well-being; for everyone who has fallen into calamity, there is no impurity even during a birth-impurity. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Dākṣa Dharmaśāstra.
The seventh chapter: That by which the world is brought under control, by which the self is brought under control, and by which the objects of the senses are conquered—that I declare to be yoga. 7.1
Breath control (prāṇāyāma), as well as meditation (dhyāna), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra),
concentration (dhāraṇā), reasoning (tarka), and absorption (samādhi)— this is said to be the six-limbed yoga.
Yoga does not arise from dwelling in the forest, nor from contemplating many books.
Yoga does not belong to anyone through vows, sacrifices, or austerities;
(7.3) nor does yoga arise from the lotus posture, nor from gazing at the tip of the nose, nor can it ever be attained through any purification other than that prescribed by the scriptures. (7.4)
Neither by silence, nor by mantras, nor by various deceptions, nor even by many meritorious deeds,
will yoga ever belong to anyone who is occupied with the affairs of the world.
But through application, through practice, and through resolute determination toward that very goal—
Through repeated detachment, the yoga of the yogi is perfected.
Through the diversion of self-reflection, through purity, through play,
and through equanimity toward all beings, yoga is perfected— and not otherwise.
He who always delights in the self, likewise plays with the self,
is constantly blissful in the self, and is ever absorbed in the self alone;
and thus, being himself content, he is satisfied and has no other mental object.
For one who is always well-satisfied, yoga becomes perfected.
Even while asleep, he remains joined in yoga, and especially so while awake;
such a practitioner is considered the best and most excellent among those who discourse on Brahman.
But he who does not perceive a second thing apart from the Self— he,
having become Brahman, is indeed described as being on the side of Dakṣa.
For one whose mind is attached to sense objects does not find yoga.
Therefore, with effort, the yogi should avoid attachment to sense objects.
Some indeed say that the union of the senses with their objects is yoga;
however, unrighteousness has been grasped as righteousness by those who are not wise.

Others likewise [teach] the union of the self and the mind; for these people have their minds turned outward and are utterly bereft of yoga. Having made the mind free from fluctuations, [one should fix it] upon the Kṣetrajña, the Supreme Self.
Having unified [the mind], one should be liberated; such a person is said to be "yoked in yoga.
The activities of the mind—such as passion, delusion, distraction, shame, and doubt—are fully described; having conquered them, one should bring them under control.
With five domestic kinsmen, he is the sixth and the greatest among them;
he cannot be conquered by gods, asuras, or humans.
Yet, one who seizes the kingdoms of others by force is not called a hero.
He by whom the collection of senses is conquered is called a hero by the wise.
Having turned all [the senses] that are directed outward toward [the self],
one should indeed yoke the entire collection of senses and the mind to the Self.

Freed from all states of being, one should place the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) within Brahman. This is both meditation and yoga; everything else is merely an expansion of books. Having abandoned the enjoyment of sense objects, the mind attains immovability.
Samādhi is proclaimed to be the very nature of the power of the Self.
The fruit resulting from the conjunction of four factors is impermanent;
however, that which results from the conjunction of two is eternal, constant, and undecaying.
To say that something which does not exist for the whole world exists is a contradiction;
when it is spoken, it does not take root in the heart of another.
For that Brahman is to be known by oneself alone, just like the sexual experience of a young maiden.
One who lacks yoga does not know it at all, just as one blind from birth cannot perceive a jar.
(7.24) For one whose nature is constant practice, that [reality] becomes self-evident;
because of its subtlety, that supreme, eternal Brahman is indefinable. (7.25)
For the wise regard women as an ornament, a burden, and like a smear of unguent; yet the fool and the simple-minded prize them highly.
All the gods are of exalted nature, yet they are all brought under control by sensual objects.
How much less, then, can this be achieved by base beings, such as humans? What talk can there be of them here?
Therefore, one who has abandoned all passions must exercise restraint;
for another, however, is unable to do so, being overwhelmed by the objects of the senses.

For just as water struck by the wind does not remain steady for even a single moment due to its waves, so too is the mind; therefore, one should not place trust in it. Many men live under the pretext of being "triple-staffed" ascetics (tridaṇḍins).
But he who does not know Brahman is not worthy of the triple staff (tridaṇḍa).

He should always protect celibacy (brahmacarya) in its eightfold form, which excludes the eight types of sexual union: remembering, speaking of, playing, looking at, secret conversation, [accepting gifts, commissioning, and consenting]. 7.30–7.31
"Intention, determination, and the actual accomplishment of the act—wise men declare this to be the eightfold sexual union.
One should never think of it, speak of it, or hear of it. (7.32)
Only one who is fully endowed with all these qualities becomes an ascetic (yati), and no other.
Furthermore, if anyone, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, persists in unrighteousness,
the king shall brand him with the mark of a dog's foot and quickly banish him from the realm.
A single monk is as described; two are considered a pair (*mithuna*);
three are known as a village (*grāma*), and more than that acts like a city (*nagara*).
Indeed, one should not establish a city, nor a village, nor likewise a pair.
A renunciant who performs these three things falls away from his own duty (svadharma).
Likewise, there will undoubtedly arise among them mutual talk of kings, talk regarding alms, affection, backbiting, and envy due to their close proximity. (7.36–7.37)
For the sake of gain and honor, there is exposition and the gathering of disciples;
these and many other such elaborations belong to those wretched ascetics.
Meditation, purity, alms-seeking, and constant adherence to solitude—these are their true marks.
For a monk there are four [grounds for] formal acts; a fifth is not possible:

one emaciated by austerities and recitations, one who is diseased, one who brings trouble to the monastery, one who is old, one who is possessed by a spirit, and any other whose faculties are impaired. (7.39–7.40)
A healthy and young monk who does not bring his own lodging [to the monastery] defiles that place and oppresses the wise.
Being both healthy and young, he perishes from his celibate life.
But one who has fallen away from the holy life (brahmacarya) shall destroy both his family and his lineage.
If a monk living in a monastery indulges in sexual intercourse, there shall be the destruction of that monastery, and he cuts down even entire families. (7.42–7.43)

If an ascetic should rest even for a moment in someone’s hermitage, what need has he for any other merit? He is born as one who has accomplished his purpose. Whatever sin has been accumulated by a householder until the end of life—
A mendicant who has fasted for one night destroys all that evil.
He who feeds a mendicant exhausted by meditation and yoga has,
in effect, fed the entire three worlds, including all things moving and stationary.
In whatever land a yogi skilled in the yoga of meditation may dwell, that land itself becomes purified; how much more so his kinsmen!
Duality, as well as non-duality, and likewise both duality and non-duality.
Neither duality nor non-duality—this is the ultimate truth. (7.48) "I am not, nor do I have any connection with another," when one is thus permeated by the state of Brahman;
in such a condition, the supreme state is attained. (7.49)
The dualistic positions have been fully explained; now I shall declare the determination of the scripture regarding those who are established in non-duality.
Here, one does not perceive a second thing whatsoever apart from the Self.
Therefore, the scriptures are studied and heard from extensive texts.
In the *Dakṣa-śāstra*, the exposition of the stages of life (*āśrama*) was proclaimed in ancient times;
those Brahmins who study them go to the world of the immortals.
The man who recites this with devotion, or even listens to it, shall possess sons, grandsons, and cattle, and shall attain great fame.
Having caused this scripture to be heard at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony, the best of the twice-born [attains the highest merit].
"The ancestral offering becomes inexhaustible and arises for the ancestors.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Dharmaśāstra of Dakṣa;
and this Saṃhitā of Dakṣa is completed.
